column1: What is the fundamental hemodynamic equation governing blood pressure?
column2: MAP = CO × SVR (Mean Arterial Pressure = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance)

column1: According to the Hagen-Poiseuille relationship, what happens to resistance if arteriolar radius decreases by 20%?
column2: Resistance doubles, because resistance scales with the fourth power of vessel radius (1/r⁴).

column1: What are the three interdependent determinants of stroke volume?
What ventricular adaptation occurs in response to chronically elevated afterload, and what downstream condition does it predispose to?
column2: Concentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in parallel, increased wall thickness), which reduces diastolic compliance and predisposes to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).

column1: What is the Windkessel effect, and what happens when it is lost with arterial aging?
column2: The Windkessel effect is the elastic reservoir function of the aorta that buffers systolic pressure and maintains diastolic flow via recoil. When lost (arterial stiffening), pulse wave velocity increases and the reflected wave returns during systole instead of diastole, amplifying systolic pressure and reducing diastolic coronary perfusion (causing isolated systolic hypertension).

column1: What percentage of hypertension cases are classified as primary (essential), and what characterizes this type?
column2: Roughly 90–95% of cases. Primary hypertension is polygenic and environmentally modulated, with no single identifiable cause, arising from cumulative small-effect genetic variants affecting renal sodium handling, RAAS, sympathetic tone, and endothelial signaling.

column1: In established hypertension, is cardiac output typically elevated or normal, and what is usually the dominant driver of elevated MAP?
column2: Cardiac output is typically normal or even reduced; markedly elevated total peripheral resistance (TPR) is the dominant driver, reflecting maturation from volume/neurohormonal dysregulation into a structural vascular disorder.

column1: Describe the RAAS cascade from renin release to angiotensin II effects.
column2: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin → cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → ACE (pulmonary endothelium) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II → angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction via AT₁ receptors, stimulates aldosterone secretion (increasing distal nephron Na+ reabsorption), and activates sympathetic tone while suppressing baroreceptor sensitivity.

column1: What is the cellular mechanism by which calcium channel blockers reduce blood pressure?
column2: They block L-type calcium channels, preventing extracellular Ca²⁺ influx into vascular smooth muscle; this reduces calmodulin activation and myosin light chain kinase phosphorylation, inhibiting actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling and causing vasodilation.

column1: What is the difference between white-coat hypertension and masked hypertension?
column2: White-coat hypertension: elevated readings in clinic due to sympathetic activation, but normal readings outside clinic. Masked hypertension: normal clinic readings falsely reassure while ambulatory/home pressures remain elevated.

column1: What diagnostic thresholds define hypertension per 2023 ESC/ESH guidelines for office vs. home monitoring?
column2: Office: SBP ≥140 mmHg and/or DBP ≥90 mmHg on repeated measurements. Home monitoring: ≥135/85 mmHg.

column1: Name four common sources of measurement error in blood pressure assessment.
column2: Cuff size mismatch (systematic bias with arm circumference), improper arm positioning (hydrostatic pressure gradients), inadequate rest period (sympathetic surge not dissipated), and observer digit preference bias in auscultatory readings.
